title: Seeing faces in things
hook: Your brain flags a face in a plug socket almost as fast as a real face.
peek: Seeing faces in clouds, cars and kettles is not a sign of an overactive imagination. Brain recordings show that face-like objects trigger the brain's face-processing regions within about a fifth of a second, nearly as quickly as real faces do.
lede: Pareidolia is the habit of seeing meaningful shapes, especially faces, in random patterns: two windows and a door on a house, the front of a car, a slice of toast. It is not a quirk of a few people. Nearly everyone does it, and brain recordings show it happens early and automatically, before we have consciously decided what we are looking at.

bullets.text: A team led by Nouchine Hadjikhani recorded brain activity as people viewed real faces, face-like objects and ordinary objects. Face-like objects stirred a face-sensitive region after about 165 milliseconds, only slightly later than real faces.
A 2020 study found the brain treats illusory faces as faces for a split second, then quickly sorts them back among objects. That is how we can see the face in a socket and still know it is a socket.
In a 2022 study, people judged hundreds of face-like objects. Most were seen as male, even though objects have no gender, which suggests our default face template leans that way.
Rhesus monkeys look longer at face-like objects than at similar objects without the face, suggesting the habit is older than our own species.
The name comes from Greek words meaning beside and image: a picture that sits alongside what is really there.
